title: India's Crude Oil Import Price Crosses $100 as Middle East Conflict Squeezes Supply Lines
excerpt: The Indian Basket benchmark hit $101.07 per barrel on Friday, its highest since May, as US-Iran hostilities disrupt Gulf shipping and freight rates soar over 400%.
body:
• India's crude oil benchmark — the Indian Basket — surged to $101.07 per barrel on Friday, crossing $100 for the first time since May as US-Iran hostilities intensified in the Persian Gulf.
  • India paid 60% more for crude imports in the April-June quarter year-on-year, and the July bill was 41% higher, driven by reduced Middle East oil flows and a 400%-plus spike in freight rates from Saudi Arabia to India.
  • Middle East crude shipments have fallen to about 11 million barrels per day from 18 million bpd before the Iran war began seven months ago, according to Argus, though alternative routes have partially offset the shortfall.
  • Indian equities fell on Tuesday, with the Sensex losing 0.73% and the Nifty dropping 0.61%, as analysts warned that sustained high oil prices could trigger a US rate hike and further pressure India's fiscal position.

India's average crude oil import price surged past $100 per barrel last week for the first time since May, as renewed hostilities between the United States and Iran disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and pushed global energy markets deeper into uncertainty.

The Indian Basket — a composite of sweet-grade Dated Brent and sour-grade Oman-Dubai benchmarks reflecting what Indian refineries actually pay — hit $101.07 per barrel on Friday, according to data from the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC) of India's oil ministry. As of Monday, the September average stood at $99.38, up sharply from $83 in June, $82 in July, and $90 in August.

War Premium and Freight Costs

The price surge is a direct consequence of more than seven months of conflict in the Middle East. Crude oil shipments from the region have fallen to about 11 million barrels per day from 18 million bpd before the war began, according to energy data firm Argus. Freight rates on the critical Ras Tanura-to-India route have soared more than 400% since February 28, when Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz.

Brent crude rose 1.4% to $98.4 per barrel on Tuesday after Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi forces said they attacked Saudi energy facilities, according to Reuters. No very large crude carrier has been visible exiting the Strait of Hormuz since September 2, Kpler tracking data showed.

"At the moment, it's telling us that physically things are incredibly tight. We've already got prices substantially above $100 a barrel and even more important, you've got a diesel market that is screaming shortage."

— David Fyfe, Chief Economist, Argus

India's Import Bill Under Pressure

India, which meets more than 85% of its crude needs through imports and is the world's third-largest oil buyer, has already absorbed a severe hit. The country paid 60% more for crude imports in the April-June quarter compared to the same period last year, even though import volumes fell 4% to 59.8 million tonnes, PPAC data showed. The trend continued into the third quarter, with July's import bill running 41% higher year-on-year.

The April-June import bill totalled $49.8 billion, up from $30.9 billion a year earlier, as elevated prices more than offset the volume decline, according to Outlook Business.

Markets React

Indian equity markets extended their losing streak on Tuesday. The BSE Sensex fell 0.73% to 75,577.58 and the Nifty 50 dropped 0.61% to 23,635.1, marking their sixth decline in seven sessions and a cumulative 2.2% loss over that period.

"Besides hurting the domestic economy, higher crude is likely to trigger a U.S. rate hike next week," said Avinash Gorakshakar, founder and head of research at Avinash Mentor Research. Heavyweight financials and private banks led the decline, with ICICI Bank and Reliance Industries each falling more than 1%.

Supply Alternatives and Demand Destruction

Gulf producers have partially adapted by rerouting exports. Saudi Aramco resumed loadings from Ras Tanura inside the Gulf in August, and exports from Egypt's Sidi Kerir port more than doubled in August compared to June, according to Kpler. Iraq's exports rebounded to about 2.34 million bpd in August.

On the demand side, China — the world's largest crude importer — slashed seaborne shipments to 7 million bpd in July and August from over 11 million bpd in February, cushioning the global shortfall. Demand destruction in petrochemicals and transportation fuels remained significant at 3.5 million bpd in the third quarter, with China accounting for more than half due to rising electrification and coal-based chemicals, according to Rystad Energy.

What's Next

Morgan Stanley expects Brent to average $100 a barrel in the fourth quarter, while Goldman Sachs raised its Brent forecast by $5 to $85 for December 2026. Physical markets are already trading above $100 — Oman futures were at $104.54 and cash Dubai at $105.10 on Monday, according to Reuters data. With the US Federal Reserve's September rate decision approaching and no sign of de-escalation in the Persian Gulf, India's energy import bill and fiscal calculus face sustained pressure in the months ahead.
